\title{One Flag and Two Gaps: What Zero-Shot\\COCO-to-Driving Detection Results Hide}
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Adithya Rajendran}
\IEEEauthorblockA{San Jos\'e State University\\CMPE 249 Intelligent Autonomous Systems, Fall 2026 (Track A)}}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
COCO-pretrained detectors lose half their AP on KITTI. We evaluate four families (YOLO26 with three
post-processing variants, RT-DETR, open-vocabulary YOLOE and the Cosmos~3 Edge VLM) zero-shot and fine-tuned, with a
devkit-faithful evaluator and paired bootstrap tests, on a Jetson Orin Nano. Three findings change how such
comparisons should be read. First, one post-processing flag reverses an AP comparison between two heads of the same
model: Ultralytics' predictor keeps one class per box, and enabling multi-label NMS adds 1.6 AP on KITTI and beats the
NMS-free head it otherwise trails. Second, the domain gap is two gaps: doubling resolution helps mainly cars under
40~px, fine-tuning mainly cars above 25~px (car AP 50.7 to 68.3). Third, 60 to 70\% of audited ``false positives''
on tiny boxes are unlabeled real objects. On nuImages the flag and the resolution effect recur, and the KITTI
fine-tune collapses (34.0 to 9.6 AP). A LoRA-tuned VLM learns the rare classes the fine-tuned detector loses and
edges it on KITTI (compact adapter 28.6 vs.\ 26.5 AP, not paired-tested; F1 0.82 for both). On the robot, a TensorRT detector runs in
16~ms; that adapter takes 6.3~s.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Robots inherit their eyes from datasets they will never see again. A mobile base or a vehicle typically runs a
detector pretrained on COCO \cite{lin2014coco} and deployed, unchanged, on its own camera. KITTI \cite{geiger2012kitti}
is the classic test of that transfer: the objects are familiar, but the viewpoint, the scale and the labeling
conventions are not. The course tutorial \cite{liu2026ngdet} reports zero-shot KITTI mAP of 0.26 to 0.28 for COCO
models on 120 frames; our closed-set models land at 0.26 to 0.28 on the full validation split under a different
protocol, and we ask what that number is made of, and what a robot can do about it on an 8~GB Jetson Orin Nano.

The answer turns out to depend as much on evaluation choices as on models, so we organize the paper around three
findings rather than a leaderboard:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Finding 1, one flag.} The NMS-free head's KITTI advantage over the NMS head (+0.7 AP, +11 AR) is
  multi-label output, not the absence of NMS. One predictor flag reverses the AP comparison and explains the gap to
  published COCO numbers (Section~\ref{sec:flag}).
  \item \textbf{Finding 2, two gaps.} Resolution recovers mainly far-field objects; in-domain fine-tuning recovers
  mainly near- and mid-field ones (Section~\ref{sec:gaps}).
  \item \textbf{Finding 3, missing labels.} Most of the small ``false positives'' that separate models are real
  objects KITTI never labeled (Section~\ref{sec:failures}).
\end{itemize}
On nuImages the flag and the resolution effect recur, and in the course tutorial's harness the same protocol switches
move results by as much as the gaps between models. The two fine-tunes behave differently: the full fine-tune of the
detector wins KITTI cars and collapses on nuImages, while LoRA on the VLM learns trucks and cyclists and edges the
detector on KITTI overall.
Around them we report the full Track~A comparison: closed-set vs.\ open-vocabulary vs.\ VLM, speed vs.\ accuracy on
the Jetson, zero-shot vs.\ fine-tuned, and a typed failure analysis. Section~\ref{sec:practice} turns the findings
into a checklist for anyone comparing detectors across datasets, and the harness, configs, manifests and logs are
public (\repourl).

\section{Background and Related Work}
\textbf{Detector families.} Two-stage detectors \cite{ren2015faster} propose regions and then classify them; dense
one-stage detectors \cite{redmon2016yolo} predict a box at every feature-map location; query-based detectors
\cite{carion2020detr,zhu2021deformable,zhao2024rtdetr} predict a fixed set. The axis that separates them is target
assignment: IoU and task-aligned matching give an object many positive anchors (one-to-many), Hungarian matching
gives it one (one-to-one).

\textbf{From NMS to end-to-end detection.} One-to-many training makes duplicates at inference, so dense detectors
need non-maximum suppression (NMS). DETR's bipartite matching removes it \cite{carion2020detr}; YOLOv10 trains a
one-to-one head alongside a one-to-many head \cite{wang2024yolov10}, and YOLO26 ships both heads on the same weights
\cite{yolo26docs}, which lets us compare them with everything else fixed. RT-DETR argues that NMS makes latency
scene-dependent \cite{zhao2024rtdetr}. Low-score boxes also matter downstream: ByteTrack recovers occluded objects
by associating detections far below the usual threshold \cite{zhang2022bytetrack}.

\textbf{Open vocabulary and VLMs.} Grounding DINO \cite{liu2024groundingdino} and YOLOE \cite{wang2025yoloe} take
class names as text prompts; general VLMs now emit boxes as text \cite{qwen3vl}. Cosmos~3 \cite{nvidia2026cosmos3}
is NVIDIA's physical-AI family, and its 2.4B Edge variant runs on the Orin Nano \cite{cosmos3edge_jetson}.

\textbf{Diagnosing errors.} Hoiem et al.\ \cite{hoiem2012diagnosing} and TIDE \cite{bolya2020tide} decompose
detector errors into localization, classification, duplicate, background and missed types; our error census adapts
their types to KITTI's ignore regions and adds a manual audit of the ``background'' type.

\subsection{Datasets and taxonomy mapping}
COCO val2017 (5{,}000 images) is the in-domain reference. KITTI 2D object detection \cite{geiger2012kitti} is
evaluated on the standard 3{,}769-frame validation half of the labeled set \cite{chen2015_3dop}: 14{,}385 cars,
2{,}280 pedestrians, 893 cyclists, 606 trucks and 287 trams. Fine-tuning uses the other 3{,}712 frames only. The
VLM comparison uses a fixed random 300-frame subset (seed 0). As a second driving domain we use 3{,}000 random
key frames (seed 0) of nuImages val \cite{caesar2020nuscenes}, which the tutorial recommends as the reliable 2D
driving benchmark. Table~\ref{tab:mapping} gives the KITTI mapping; the nuImages mapping follows the same rules and
is in the repository.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{KITTI-to-COCO mapping. ``Ignore'' boxes are neither true positives nor false positives.}
\label{tab:mapping}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.3cm}p{5.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
KITTI & Treatment \\
\midrule
Car, Pedestrian, Truck, Tram & COCO car, person, truck, train \\
Van, Person\_sitting & ignored for car / person, IoU-matched (devkit neighboring classes) \\
Cyclist & ignored for person, matched by containment (a COCO person box covers only the rider); a real class for open-vocabulary models and the fine-tuned model \\
DontCare & ignore region for all classes (intersection over detection area) \\
Misc & dropped \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Evaluation protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
Every model is scored by one pycocotools-based evaluator \cite{cocoapi} that applies the ignore rules. Detectors run
with NMS IoU 0.7 and at most 300 boxes per image; AP runs keep boxes down to confidence 0.001 and score the top 100
per image (pycocotools maxDets); the deployment operating point is confidence 0.25. We report
COCO metrics (AP, AP$_{50}$, AP$_{75}$, AP$_{S/M/L}$, AR$_{100}$, per-class AP), AP by box height in pixels, and
KITTI-style AP$|_{R40}$ at the devkit IoU (0.7 for vehicles, 0.5 for pedestrians and cyclists). Intervals are 95\%
image-level percentile bootstrap intervals \cite{efron1993bootstrap} (200 resamples for single models, 300 for the VLM
runs); differences between two models use a paired bootstrap (300 to 500 resamples, the same image weights applied
to both), which our tests show reproduces pycocotools exactly at unit weights. The VLM returns no scores; for AP and
AR we score each box by the geometric-mean probability of the tokens that spell it, but because those scores are not
calibrated like a detector's we also compare the VLM by precision, recall and F1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 with every box.
Closed-set models get a rule-based cyclist (a person box over a bicycle box). Latency is measured at batch 1 on 500
KITTI frames after 50 warm-up frames, at confidence 0.25, synchronized, from decoded image to boxes; peak memory is
the PyTorch allocator peak (unified memory has no per-process counter).

\subsection{Hardware, software and reproducibility}
All detector runs, the detector fine-tunes and every latency number use a Jetson Orin Nano Super 8~GB (JetPack 6.2.3,
L4T R36.5.2) in MAXN\_SUPER mode with clocks locked by
\texttt{jetson\_clocks} (GPU 1.02~GHz, EMC 3.2~GHz), torch 2.10, Ultralytics 8.4.183 \cite{ultralytics} and
TensorRT 10.3 FP16 engines; Cosmos~3 Edge runs in BF16 through Hugging Face Transformers. Inference is FP16; on
1{,}000 COCO images FP32 gives 54.28 AP and FP16 54.16, so precision is not a factor. Fine-tuning ran in the
Ultralytics JetPack~6 container (same Ultralytics and torch versions). The VLM adapters were trained, and all VLM
accuracy numbers computed, on an ASUS Ascent GX10 (NVIDIA GB10, 128~GB unified memory) with Transformers at commit
60f4954. Greedy decoding keeps the two machines close but not identical: the zero-shot run gives 1{,}035 true and
648 false positives at IoU 0.5 on the Orin Nano and 1{,}043 and 668 on the GX10, the same F1 (0.66). Tables~\ref{tab:vlmft} and~\ref{tab:vlm}
use the GX10 run; the error census (Table~\ref{tab:failures}) and label audit use the Orin Nano run. VLM latencies are measured on the Orin Nano in a container with the same versions. Every
run writes a manifest with its command, settings, versions and machine; Table~\ref{tab:repro} lists them.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Baseline and reproduction}
Table~\ref{tab:main} gives the main results. COCO AP of 52 to 53 falls to 26 to 28 on KITTI for every closed-set
model; YOLOE falls to 22 on the same four classes (its 18.4 in Table~\ref{tab:main} also averages its own cyclist
class). RT-DETR-l reproduces its published COCO number to within 0.3 AP and the NMS-free YOLO26m head to within 0.3,
but the NMS head scores 52.2 against a published 53.1. That gap is the first clue to Finding~1.

\textit{Course harness.} We also ran the tutorial's own \texttt{run\_eval} \cite{liu2026ngdet} unmodified on the
Orin Nano (Table~\ref{tab:ngdet}). Its exact command gives 23.6 to 24.0 mAP against the published 26.2 to 27.9.
Lowering the score threshold to 0.001 adds 0.2 to 1.2, and using 1,000 frames instead of 120 moves the numbers by
under 0.7; neither closes the 2 to 4 point gap, which we attribute to the frame sample, hardware and library
versions without being able to separate them. Three protocol switches, applied to a separate patched copy that matches the
original exactly when they are off, each change the result by about as much as the gaps between models. Treating
KITTI DontCare regions as ignore regions, as the devkit does, adds 0.5 to 1.1 mAP to every model. Splitting the
merged \emph{vehicle} class into car and truck (\texttt{driving5}) is what makes multi-label NMS matter: it adds 0.6
mAP and 7.7 AR there and nothing under \texttt{driving3}, where a car/truck duplicate is the same class. The switches
reorder the models: RT-DETR-R50 narrowly leads under the tutorial's protocol, YOLO26x with multi-label NMS under the
five-class one. Under both taxonomies cyclist AP is 0.0 for every model, because a COCO \emph{bicycle} box never
matches a KITTI \emph{Cyclist} box drawn around rider and bicycle; a third of the \texttt{driving3} mean is fixed at
zero, which our rider-plus-bicycle composition (Table~\ref{tab:mapping}) avoids.

\subsection{Finding 1: one flag decides the head comparison in AP}\label{sec:flag}
On COCO the NMS and NMS-free heads tie (52.2 vs.\ 52.2). On KITTI the NMS-free head is ahead by a small but
significant 0.7 AP and 11.0 points of class-averaged AR$_{100}$ (Table~\ref{tab:paired}). We expected the reason to
be NMS deleting overlapping parked cars. It is not: per class, recall with every box kept rises by 30 points for
trucks (0.61 to 0.90) and 17 for trams, but only 1.8 for cars, and the error census shows no fewer ``crowded''
misses. At the 0.25 deployment threshold the heads are indistinguishable (recall 0.812 vs.\ 0.806).

The mechanism is in post-processing. The NMS-free head takes its top-$k$ over (anchor, class) pairs, so one anchor
can be reported as both ``car'' and ``truck''. Ultralytics' \texttt{predict()} runs NMS on the arg-max class only,
while its validator, which produced the published numbers, runs NMS with \texttt{multi\_label=True}. Enabling that
one flag in the predictor:
\begin{itemize}
  \item lifts truck recall from 0.61 to 0.90 and tram recall from 0.46 to 0.66, matching the NMS-free head;
  \item adds 1.6 AP and 9.5 AR on KITTI, and beats the NMS-free head by 0.9 AP (paired interval $-$1.15 to $-$0.57
  for NMS-free minus multi-label) while trailing it by 1.6 AR;
  \item raises our COCO number from 52.2 to 52.8. Ultralytics' own validator gives 53.0 (NMS) and 52.5 (NMS-free) on
  the same weights, matching the published 53.1 and 52.5; the last 0.2 is batching and letterboxing.
\end{itemize}
At the 0.25 deployment threshold the flag changes little (precision and recall 0.70 / 0.82 with it, 0.71 / 0.81
without), and multi-label output can report one object under two labels, which a downstream tracker must handle; the
finding is about AP and AR, the metrics comparisons are usually made on.
The flag matters more on KITTI than on COCO because KITTI's vans and box trucks sit on COCO's car/truck boundary;
the NMS-free head already leads by 3.3 truck AP on COCO itself (Fig.~\ref{fig:nmsgap}). The NMS-free head keeps a
real advantage, latency: under TensorRT it runs at 15.6~ms p50 against 18.0~ms for the arg-max NMS head
(Table~\ref{tab:latency}), almost all of it the NMS step; we did not time multi-label NMS, which is likely slower. Neither head's latency depends on scene clutter with clocks locked (Fig.~\ref{fig:latency}).
On nuImages, where cars, trucks and buses are all labeled classes, the same flag adds 0.6 AP and 5.1 AR (33.2 to
33.7 AP, 45.1 to 50.2 AR; trucks +0.7, buses +0.8), and the NMS-free head again ties the arg-max NMS head on AP
(33.2) with even higher recall (51.7 AR). The direction recurs on a second dataset with its own labeling
conventions, at about a third of KITTI's size; we did not run a paired test on nuImages, so this is a point
estimate.

\subsection{Finding 2: the domain gap is two gaps}\label{sec:gaps}
Doubling the input from 640 to 1280~px raises KITTI AP by 2.4 for the NMS head (paired interval +1.8 to +3.1).
Fig.~\ref{fig:height} shows where: on cars under 25~px tall, YOLO26m gains 7.5 AP (44.8 to 52.3) and YOLOE 9.6; on
25 to 40~px cars 3.4; above 40~px nothing (59.6 vs.\ 58.9 above 80~px). With KITTI's focal length of about
720~px, a 1.5~m tall car is 25~px tall at roughly 43~m, so resolution is a far-field fix. (Small rare classes gain
too: trucks 25 to 40~px tall rise 14 AP, on few boxes.) We plot cars because
they are the only class with enough small objects: the split has 32 pedestrians and 10 trams under 25~px, and
class-averaged height-bin AP is dominated by that noise.

The near field is the larger loss, and it is localization. On COCO YOLO26m keeps 75\% of its AP$_{50}$ at
AP$_{50:95}$ (52.2 / 69.5); on KITTI it keeps 52\% (26.2 / 50.1). At the deployment threshold, 48\% of its misses
are ``loose'' (a box on the object at IoU below 0.5): large near cars, often truncated at the border, get covered
by partial boxes (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}a). Fine-tuning removes this part. At 640~px, car AP rises from 59.6 to
81.1 above 80~px, from 48.9 to 68.9 at 40 to 80~px and from 49.5 to 60.5 at 25 to 40~px, but cars under 25~px do not
move (44.8 vs.\ 45.6). On the subset at confidence 0.25, loose misses fall from 149 to 13, though total misses do
not (328 vs.\ 333): the fine-tuned model trades loose boxes for occluded, crowded and outright misses as it emits
fewer low-confidence boxes. In-domain data fixes near- and mid-field localization; only more pixels fix the far
field.

\subsection{Fine-tuning: what a night on the robot buys}
YOLO26m was fine-tuned from the COCO checkpoint on 3{,}412 KITTI training frames (300 more held out for checkpoint
selection) with five classes named as in COCO (car, person, cyclist, truck, train), which lets Ultralytics copy the
pretrained classifier rows for four of them. Training ran for a fixed 7-hour budget (84 epochs) at 640~px, batch 8,
on the Orin Nano itself. YOLO training has no ignore regions, so Van, Person\_sitting, Misc and DontCare are
background; evaluation still uses the devkit rules. Ultralytics' score on the held-out training frames reached
0.79 AP, but those frames share drives with the training frames; Table~\ref{tab:finetune} uses the validation split.

The result is mixed in an informative way (Table~\ref{tab:finetune}). Cars, with 13{,}195 training boxes, improve
from 50.7 to 68.3 AP and from 74.7 to 90.6 KITTI moderate AP$|_{R40}$, and subset F1 rises from 0.73 to 0.84 as
precision jumps from 0.68 to 0.92. Trucks and trams, with 450 and 206 training boxes, regress (11.3 to 8.0 and 18.5
to 10.3 AP), the forgetting the tutorial also reports for small per-domain sets \cite{liu2026ngdet}. Pedestrians gain
2.6 COCO-style AP but lose 7 KITTI moderate AP at IoU 0.5, and AR drops because the fine-tuned model emits far fewer
low-score boxes. The class-averaged gain is only +2.2 AP (paired interval +0.9 to +3.3), which hides a large car gain
behind two rare-class regressions. We hypothesized that training on Vans as background teaches the model not to fire
on van-shaped trucks; an ablation that grays out Van and Person\_sitting regions during training tests this.
It supports it for trucks (one run per arm). With the same budget, seed and frames, masking the 1{,}251 Van and Person\_sitting
regions more than doubles truck AP (8.0 to 18.1; KITTI moderate 5.6 to 20.9) and raises the 4-class AP from 28.4
to 30.6 (bootstrap intervals [27.5, 29.5] and [29.7, 31.8]), while cars (68.3 vs.\ 68.4) and people (26.9 vs.\ 26.2)
do not move and trams stay low (9.8). Part of the truck loss is likely the training labels contradicting the
evaluation rules: a box that KITTI evaluation ignores was a hard negative in training. Trams, with no such neighbor
class, look like plain data scarcity.

\subsection{Closed-set, open-vocabulary and VLM}
Table~\ref{tab:vlm} compares all families on the 300-frame subset. Cosmos~3 Edge parses cleanly (297 of 300 replies
valid JSON, 3 salvaged) and finds 71\% of objects, but at 0.61 precision its F1 is 0.66, against 0.73 for YOLO26m
and 0.84 fine-tuned, and its boxes are looser (F1 at IoU 0.7: 0.49 vs.\ 0.57). On the Orin Nano it takes 17.3~s per
frame at the median (p90 36~s), about 1{,}100 times the TensorRT detector (Fig.~\ref{fig:speedacc}). YOLOE-26m is
the most precise zero-shot model (0.78) but the least complete (recall 0.61); on the four shared classes it trails
the closed-set YOLO26m by 3.8 AP on KITTI (22.4 vs.\ 26.2), yet it has the best zero-shot truck AP (20.8 vs.\ 11 to
14), plausibly because a text prompt does not inherit COCO's car/truck boundary.

No method covers cyclists, the class COCO lacks. Cosmos~3 Edge finds 11\%, mostly because it boxes the rider as a
pedestrian (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}e); YOLOE, prompted with ``cyclist'', finds none above 0.25. The zero-cost rule on a
closed-set detector reaches 24 to 33\% recall, and 681 labeled training cyclists move the fine-tuned model to only
26\% at the deployment threshold, though its cyclist AP (18.9) is the best of any detector.

\textit{Fine-tuning the VLM.} We trained LoRA adapters \cite{hu2022lora} (rank 16 on the language model's attention
and MLP projections, 4 epochs over the same 3{,}412 frames, Van and Person\_sitting as background like the detector)
on the GX10 in two output formats:
the JSON the zero-shot model already emits, and a compact one, one \texttt{label x1 y1 x2 y2} line per object,
nearest first, which halves the tokens per answer. To give the VLM AP and AR at all, each box is scored by the
geometric-mean probability of the tokens that spell it (not calibrated like detector scores, Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, so we
report F1 alongside). Table~\ref{tab:vlmft} has the result. LoRA more than doubles AP (14.4 to 32.4 on the subset)
and lifts F1 from 0.66 to 0.85, level with the fine-tuned detector's 0.84. On the full validation split the JSON
adapter reaches 30.1 AP and the compact one 28.6, against 26.5 for the fine-tuned YOLO26m on the same five-class
ground truth; F1 is 0.83, 0.82 and 0.82, so by the threshold-free and the deployment metric alike the models are
close, and the difference is in the classes. YOLO26m-FT stays ahead on cars (KITTI moderate 90.6 vs.\ 81.5) and
level on pedestrians (63.3 vs.\ 62.4); the adapted VLM learns the rare classes the detector loses, trucks (47.7 vs.\
5.6 KITTI moderate AP; zero-shot the VLM had 24.9 on the subset), cyclists (49.4 vs.\ 34.1) and trams (21.4 vs.\
18.7). We cannot attribute this
to LoRA itself: model size, pretraining data and input resolution all differ between the two models, and the masked-Van
detector already recovers 20.9 KITTI moderate truck AP. The compact format gives up 1.5 AP, about 0.9 of it on pedestrians, for
half the latency; capping it
at 128 tokens costs nothing in AP and another 12\%, and at 64 tokens recall halves because the answer is cut before
the far objects. On the Orin Nano, where decoding runs at a flat 13 tokens per second, latency follows
answer length: on the same 50 frames the compact adapter takes 6.3~s per frame (p90 11.3~s), the JSON adapter 11.6~s
and the zero-shot model 19.1~s. Fine-tuning made the VLM both more accurate and 3$\times$ faster on the robot, but it
is still 350 times slower than the detector. (Table~\ref{tab:vlm}'s 17.3~s is the zero-shot median over all 300
frames; their mean, 19.3~s, matches the 19.1~s here.)

\subsection{Speed and memory on the robot}
TensorRT FP16 halves YOLO latency and cuts RT-DETR's by almost 3$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:latency}). Every detector
fits in under 150~MB of allocator memory, so the Orin Nano's 8~GB is not the constraint for detection; it is for the
VLM, which needs the whole board. RT-DETR-l is within about 1 AP of every YOLO26m head on KITTI (its lead over the
NMS-free head is not significant, Table~\ref{tab:paired}) at twice the latency.

\subsection{Second domain: nuImages}
nuImages (3{,}000 random validation key frames from six cameras in Boston and Singapore, 1600$\times$900, mapped with
the same ignore rules) tests whether the findings are KITTI artifacts. Table~\ref{tab:nuimages} has the results.
Zero-shot, the closed-set models land within 0.5 AP of each other (33.2 to 33.7), RT-DETR-l again just ahead of the
default YOLO26m heads and just behind the multi-label one. The multi-label effect of Finding~1 recurs
(Section~\ref{sec:flag}). The resolution half of Finding~2 partly recurs: at 1280~px YOLO26m gains 4.9 AP overall,
and on cars 9.7 AP under 25~px, 9.6 at 25 to 40~px, 4.8 at 40 to 80~px and $-$1.6 above 80~px. The gain still
shrinks with size and vanishes for the nearest cars, but unlike KITTI it reaches mid-size objects, plausibly because
nuImages' 1600~px frames are downscaled 2.5$\times$ at 640~px input against KITTI's 1.9$\times$. The fine-tuning half
cannot be tested here without a nuImages fine-tune.

The KITTI fine-tune does not transfer; it collapses. AP on the three classes both models share falls from 34.0 to
9.6, and every height bin drops, near cars included (69.4 to 43.6 above 80~px). The model did not break: at
confidence 0.25 it is 92\% precise but recalls 16\% of objects, and even at confidence 0.001 it emits 4 boxes per
nuImages frame against 72 for the COCO checkpoint. Seven hours of full fine-tuning on 3{,}412 frames from one camera in one city made it
confident only on KITTI-looking objects. The masked-Van model behaves the same (10.6). For a robot that will leave
its training city, the KITTI gains in Table~\ref{tab:finetune} are not free; replay of the original data, a lower
learning rate or a low-rank update are the standard remedies, which we did not test.

\section{Failure Analysis and Finding 3: what the labels miss}\label{sec:failures}
Every error at the deployment threshold gets one type (Table~\ref{tab:failures}; definitions follow
\cite{hoiem2012diagnosing,bolya2020tide} and are in \texttt{det\_eval/failures.py}). Loose localization is the largest
category for every zero-shot model, in both misses and false positives, and the one fine-tuning removes. RT-DETR-l's
higher recall comes with nearly three times YOLO26m's false positives at the same threshold because its scores are
calibrated lower: a shared threshold means something different for each model.

The ``tiny, unlabeled'' type deserves its own finding. KITTI marks some distant regions DontCare but leaves many
distant objects unlabeled. In random samples of 30 such false positives, 21 of YOLO26m's (70\%, Wilson interval 52
to 83\%) and 18 of Cosmos's (60\%, 42 to 75\%) were real unlabeled vehicles or people (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}d).
Cosmos has 246 of these on the subset against YOLO26m's 79, so the metric penalizes it most: correcting for the
audit, its precision is closer to 0.70 than 0.61, while YOLO26m's moves only from 0.68 to about 0.72. The genuine hallucinations differ by model: YOLO26m calls
roadside delineator posts and barriers ``person'' (4 of its 8; Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}c), a phantom-braking risk;
Cosmos boxes signs, bollards and parts of labeled cars. Taxonomy drives the ``confused'' type: COCO calls a delivery
van a truck, KITTI calls it a Van, and the devkit ignores Van only for car (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}b).

\section{Recommendations for Cross-Dataset Detection Comparisons}\label{sec:practice}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Fix and report the post-processing.} State whether NMS is multi-label; with Ultralytics, compare
  heads under the same setting or the comparison measures the flag, not the head.
  \item \textbf{Reproduce in-domain first.} A 0.9 AP COCO gap was the clue to item 1.
  \item \textbf{Score with the target dataset's ignore rules.} Without DontCare and neighbor classes, KITTI
  charges every model for objects it was never asked to find.
  \item \textbf{Report per-class and per-height results, and test differences with a paired bootstrap.} Class means
  hide an 18-point car gain behind two rare-class regressions, and class-averaged small-object AP can rest on ten
  objects.
  \item \textbf{Audit the background errors before ranking.} Sixty to seventy percent of tiny false positives here
  were real objects.
  \item \textbf{Report a threshold-free metric next to any shared threshold.} A shared confidence threshold is not a
  shared precision: at 0.25, RT-DETR-l has nearly three times YOLO26m's false positives (Table~\ref{tab:failures}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Limitations}
One board for inference, and VLM confidences come from token probabilities, which are not calibrated like detector
scores. Mapping choices matter: Van is ignored only for car. Each fine-tune is one run with default hyperparameters,
a baseline rather than a tuned result, with no repeated seeds; the VLM adapters were not evaluated on nuImages, so
whether they transfer better than the detector is open, and the detector-vs-VLM comparison confounds model size,
pretraining and the fine-tuning method. nuImages results are point estimates without paired tests. The label audit covers 60 boxes and quantifies, but does not correct, KITTI's
missing labels. Latency is measured with locked clocks and may differ under thermal throttling.

\section{Conclusion}
Zero-shot COCO-to-driving numbers hide one flag and two gaps. The NMS-free head's KITTI AP advantage is multi-label
output, which an NMS head gets from one setting, and its lasting benefit is 2.4~ms of latency over the arg-max NMS
head. Resolution recovers mainly far-field cars; a night of fine-tuning on the robot recovers near- and mid-field cars
(50.7 to 68.3 AP) but not far ones, and that fine-tune collapses on nuImages. Zero-shot, a 2.4B VLM trails a
20M-parameter detector by 0.07 F1 and three orders of magnitude in speed; after LoRA on the same frames its compact
adapter matches the fine-tuned detector in F1 (0.82), edges it in AP (28.6 vs.\ 26.5) and learns the trucks and
cyclists the detector misses, at 6.3~s per frame on the robot. That makes it a candidate teacher for the detector,
not a replacement.

\section*{AI Tool Use}
As the assignment allows, Claude (Anthropic) assisted with writing the evaluation harness, debugging the Jetson and
GX10 setups, and drafting this report. Result Tables IV to VI, VIII, IX, XI and XII are generated from the run
outputs by \texttt{det\_eval.paper\_tables}; Tables III, VII and X were transcribed from \texttt{results/ngdet\_repro/},
\texttt{results/metrics/} and \texttt{results/vlm\_latency\_jetson/}. The evaluator is covered by unit tests against
pycocotools, and the label audit was judged by inspecting each crop. AI explanations were wrong several times and the
data caught them: the first explanation of Finding~1 was that NMS deletes overlapping parked cars, which per-class
recall disproved (cars gained 1.8 points, trucks 30); a class-averaged height-bin plot suggested a small-object effect
that rested on 10 trams, so the figure became car-only; an early summary misreported how much the course harness
moves with its score threshold; and the nuImages collapse was first treated as a possible bug and checked against box
counts before it was reported. An independent AI review of a draft against the repository found stale VLM numbers,
an unfair YOLOE comparison and overstated claims; a second review caught a false claim in the first round of
fixes (that the VLM's outputs were identical across machines). All are corrected here.
